sources.title: Grey rhebok
sources.note: Cites the 2017 IUCN assessment (Taylor, Cowell and Drouilly) of Near Threatened.

size.note: Mass is given as 19–30 kg in one compilation and 20–30 kg in another; both are recorded and are not averaged, and the wider published range is stored. Length 1.15–1.25 m is given in one account but is not stated as head-and-body versus total length, so it is stored as lengthCm only. Male horn length is given as 15–25 cm in one compilation and 20–25 cm in another. No shoulder height or tail length was found.

summary: A medium-sized antelope with a woolly grey coat, a long neck, very long pointed ears and white underparts. Only males have straight, sharp horns. It lives on rocky hills and grassy mountain slopes, and is listed as Near Threatened in the region.
description: A medium-sized antelope with a long neck and very long, pointed, erect ears, and no bare patch below the ear. The coat is short and dense, woollier and curlier than that of other antelopes, and coloured in various shades of grey; one account calls the upperparts brownish grey. The face and legs are yellowish in that account, and the underparts and tail are white. The eyes are black-lidded and stand out against a white surround. The muzzle is long and narrow, ending in a small mouth, and a naked swollen area around the nostrils extends up the nose. Only males have horns: straight or slightly bent forward, upright, sharp, and ringed at the base, with published lengths of 15–25 cm in one compilation and 20–25 cm in another. Females have four teats and no horns.
habits: Active during the day in bouts of feeding and resting, and tends to rest in the shade around noon. It is territorial. The social system is female-defence polygyny: a territorial male defends a harem in a stable herd. Sources disagree on group size and are not averaged: one account gives a harem of two to seven females plus accompanying young; another gives herds of one to 15 females and young with one mature male; a third gives a typical group of about eight animals, sometimes as many as 30. Non-territorial males are generally solitary. Males become extremely aggressive during the breeding season, and harem defence includes postural displays, snorting, stamping and serious fighting. A sentinel may give a warning grunt and lead the group onto more rugged ground. The gait is described as jerky and rocking, and the species is an agile climber and jumper. Home range size is estimated at 30–100 ha in the eastern Free State mountain grasslands. Seasonal movement between protected areas and adjacent farmland is described from the Western Cape and the southern Drakensberg; a Kruger-specific movement account was not found.

diet.summary: Predominantly a browser, often feeding on ground-hugging forbs, especially the flowers and leaves. One faecal analysis found dicotyledons made up 88% of the diet, over 90% in winter, with dicotyledon use falling by about 10% in summer. Another account describes the diet as grasses and leaves. The species is largely water-independent and obtains most of its water from its food.

young: It is a seasonal breeder. One account places mating in April and births in November and December, early in the warm, wet season, after a gestation of about 8.7 months (also given as 261 days). A single calf is born and is generally hidden away from the mother in rocks, caves or bushes for the first few months. Sources disagree on when young males leave the natal group and are not averaged: one account says males become mature at about 18–21 months and then leave; another says male offspring disperse as yearlings and remain peripheral until they gain a territory. A Kruger-specific birth-month range was not found.

predators.note: Named at family level (Hyaeninae) in the source used.
Named only as jackals in the source used.
Named as a predator; not a mammal in this guide.

habitat: Associated with rocky hills, grassy mountain slopes and plateau grasslands in the eastern part of its range, and with the rocky hills of mountain fynbos and the Little Karoo in the south and southwest. It typically inhabits grassy montane country, usually above 1,000 m, but also occurs in the Cape coastal belt almost at sea level. It needs good grass cover in the home range for shelter, but often feeds on steep open slopes with little cover. A Kruger-specific habitat account was not found.

similar.note: Grey rhebok is told by its woolly grey coat, very long pointed erect ears, and the absence of a bare patch below the ear. Only male grey rhebok have straight or slightly forward-bent horns.
Grey rhebok has a woolly grey coat, very long pointed erect ears, and no bare patch below the ear. Only males have straight or slightly forward-bent horns.

population.notes: No Kruger population figure was found. The species is on the official 2011 checklist. The 2025 regional assessment does not mention Kruger; it gives a regional minimum of 2,000 individuals in formally protected areas and says further research is needed to determine whether there are over 10,000 across the range. An earlier compilation suggested a total of about 18,000 in 1999. Those regional totals are not a park census. Regional Red List status is Near Threatened, with a declining regional trend. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf

viewNotes.note: A long neck, a woolly grey coat, very long pointed erect ears, white underparts and a white tail. The face and legs may appear yellowish. Only the male has straight, upright horns.
Very long, pointed, erect ears and no bare patch below the ear. Males show straight, upright horns; the eyes stand out against a white surround.

sources.title: Grey Rhebok
sources.note: Afrikaans name given as Vaal Ribbok; the 2011 checklist form Vaalribbok is used in this file. Regional status, range, habitat, diet and social system. Movement patterns are listed as territorial year-round and non-migratory. Mpumalanga: still occurs in Songimvelo Nature Reserve and is no longer present in Ohrigstad Nature Reserve. Limpopo: may occur in the Waterberg and the northern escarpment (Wolkberg Mountains). Does not mention Kruger or the Lowveld.

research.note: The official 2011 checklist includes this species, but the 2025 regional assessment does not mention Kruger, and no Kruger census figure was found. The 2025 assessment lists movement patterns as territorial year-round and non-migratory. It records the species in Mpumalanga at Songimvelo Nature Reserve (no longer at Ohrigstad Nature Reserve) and says it may occur in Limpopo in the Waterberg and the northern escarpment (Wolkberg Mountains); it does not describe the range as covering the Lowveld of Mpumalanga or Limpopo. iNaturalist has 1 casual observation in place 69020 (2016, no photograph) and 0 research-grade records. Status and monthsPresent are omitted rather than guessed. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf. Sources disagree on mass, horn length, group size and the age at which young males leave the natal group; both accounts are kept and are not averaged. No licensable Kruger photograph or recording was found; the five photographs used are from the Western Cape and are captioned with those places. Status pass, 22 November 2026, Africa/Johannesburg: the only Kruger mention in the 2016 assessment is the bibliography line Kettlitz (1962), on the distribution of some large game animals in the Transvaal (excluding the Kruger National Park). That line is not a park record, and the assessment does not name the Lowveld. The 2011 checklist was not used on its own. Status and monthsPresent remain omitted.

Sources disagree on mass (19–30 kg versus 20–30 kg), male horn length (15–25 cm versus 20–25 cm), group size (a harem of 2–7 females plus young versus 1–15 females and young plus one male versus about 8, up to 30), and when young males leave the natal group (at 18–21 months versus as yearlings); both accounts are recorded and are not averaged.
No shoulder height or tail length was found. The 1.15–1.25 m length figure is not stated as head-and-body versus total length.

No licensable Kruger photograph was found. A Commons search for Pelea capreolus in Kruger returned 0 hits. iNaturalist has 0 observations with photos in place 69020. The five photographs used are from the Western Cape.

iNaturalist has 0 sound observations for Pelea capreolus in place 69020. No reusable Kruger recording was found. Call types are limited to the alarm grunt and male snorting described in compiled accounts.

Iris colour, ear colour, horn colour, a sourced tail shape, and a sourced mane were not given in the sources used, so those marks are null. Calf coat marks were not found, so no calf variant was added.
No Kruger-specific habitat account or birth-month range was found.
Skinner & Chimimba and Stuart's field guide were not available as direct reads. Size, diet, habits, young, calls and predators were taken from Wikipedia, Animal Diversity Web and the EWT assessment.
